test_title: PYST 54: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 21 Dec, 2025 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: Which of the following statements about sound propagation is true?

options.text: Sound is the fastest in gases, slower in liquids and the slowest in solids.
Sound is the fastest in solids, slower in liquids and the slowest in gases.
Sound can travel in a vacuum.
Sound travels at the same speed in all mediums.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Sound is the fastest in solids, slower in liquids and the slowest in gases.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sound** is a **mechanical wave** that requires a **material medium** (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through a vacuum.
 
• The speed of sound depends on the **elasticity** and **density** of the medium. In **solids**, the molecules are **tightly packed** and held together by strong **intermolecular forces**, allowing vibrations to transfer very rapidly. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• In **liquids**, the molecules are less tightly packed than in solids but more so than in gases. Consequently, sound travels **slower in liquids** than in solids but **faster than in gases**. For example, the speed of sound in **water** is approximately **1480 m/s**.
 
• In **gases**, molecules are far apart, meaning the collisions between them occur less frequently, which results in the **slowest speed of propagation**. For instance, in **air** at **20°C**, sound travels at approximately **343 m/s**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• Sound cannot travel through a **vacuum** because there are no particles to carry the vibrations. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• The speed of sound is **not the same** in all mediums; it varies significantly based on the **physical state** and **temperature** of the substance. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nature of Sound Waves**: 
 
 
• Sound waves are **longitudinal waves**, meaning the particles of the medium vibrate **parallel** to the direction of the wave's propagation.
 
• In solids, sound can also travel as **transverse waves**, but in fluids (liquids and gases), they are primarily longitudinal.
 
 
 
• **Effect of Temperature**:
 
 
• The speed of sound **increases** with an increase in **temperature**. For example, in air, the speed increases by approximately **0.6 meters per second** for every **1 degree Celsius** rise in temperature.
 
• This happens because higher temperatures increase the **kinetic energy** of the molecules, leading to more frequent collisions.
 
 
 
• **Elasticity vs. Density**:
 
 
• While higher **density** usually tends to slow down sound, the significantly higher **elasticity** (bulk modulus) of solids more than compensates for their density, resulting in the **highest speeds** in materials like **steel** (approx **5960 m/s**) or **aluminum** (approx **6420 m/s**).
 
 
 
• **Historical Context and Applications**:
 
 
• The **Bell Jar Experiment** is a classic scientific demonstration used to prove that sound cannot travel in a **vacuum**.
 
• Understanding sound propagation is essential in fields like **SONAR** (Sound Navigation and Ranging) used by **submarines**, medical **ultrasonography**, and **seismology** to study **Earth's interior**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Human Hearing Range**: The human ear can typically hear frequencies between **20 Hz and 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)**.
 
• **Infrasonic and Ultrasonic**: Sounds with frequencies below **20 Hz** are called **infrasonic** (often produced by **elephants** or **whales**), while frequencies above **20,000 Hz** are **ultrasonic** (used by **bats** for navigation).
 
• **Mach Number**: This is the ratio of the speed of an object to the speed of sound in the surrounding medium. If an aircraft travels faster than sound, it is called **supersonic**, which produces a **sonic boom**.
